opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The name is really a blend of two ideas: "inference" and "architect," or you could also hear "perfect" in there.

Inference is the core of what we do. Training gets most of the headlines, but once a model is trained, nearly all the real-world compute goes into inference: serving the model to users, millions of times a day. That's where cost, latency, and reliability actually matter to people. So we wanted the word inference to be front and center.

The "-ect" part is about architecture. We don't see inference as a single trick or a kernel optimization here and there. It's a full-stack systems problem. You have to think about scheduling, memory management, the KV cache, how you batch requests, how you distribute across GPUs and across different kinds of hardware. You have to design that whole system the way an architect designs a building, where every piece fits together.

And honestly, there's a bit of aspiration in it too: making inference as close to perfect as we can, meaning efficient, fast, cheap, and easy enough for everyone to use. A lot of that thinking comes from my experience in the open-source community, working on inference engines. We saw how much demand there is, and how much room there still is to improve. So the name is a reminder to ourselves of what we're building toward.

r001.rationale: The response describes inference as serving trained models in real-world use and says the company is building systems to make that inference efficient and accessible, conveying an ambition to put inference into practice.

fable-5.1.text:
The name is really a combination of two words: "inference" and "architect." We thought about this for a long time, because a name is the first thing people see, and we wanted it to say what we actually do rather than something abstract.

The "inference" part is straightforward. The whole company is built around inference, around the moment a model is actually serving people, not training. My own background is in that layer. When I was working on vLLM, what I kept seeing was that training gets most of the attention and most of the glory, but inference is where the cost lives and where the user experience lives. Every token someone reads from a model goes through an inference system. So we wanted that word right up front.

The "architect" part is about how we want to approach it. There is a difference between writing a fast kernel and designing a system. A lot of the hard problems in inference today are not about one operator being slow. They are about how scheduling, memory, parallelism across machines, and the model itself all fit together. That is an architectural problem. We want to be the people who design the whole structure, not just optimize one brick. So "Inferect" is meant to say: we are the architects of inference.

There is also a smaller thing I like about it. If you say it fast, it sounds a bit like "infer" and "correct" or "infer" and "erect," like building something up. We did not plan that, but I think it fits. Inference systems today are still somewhat fragile and hand-tuned. We want to build something that stands on its own, that is solid, that people can rely on the way they rely on a database or an operating system.

So that is what we hoped the name would convey: a focus on inference as a discipline in itself, and an ambition to design the system as a whole rather than patch it piece by piece.

r001.rationale: The response links the name to inference in production—where models serve people—and to the ambition to build and architect complete inference systems.

astra-6.text: We wanted Inferect to put inference at the center—the part where a model actually becomes useful to people. The name was meant to feel focused and practical: helping people turn AI capabilities into something they can run reliably and efficiently.

r001.rationale: The response says Inferect puts inference at the center and helps turn AI capabilities into something people can run, conveying the ambition to put inference into action.
